| **CreativeMode** | Java + Bedrock mobs, items, blocks, structures, full mods | 300 free coins/week; Pro tier (VERIFIED creativemode.net header; compare page) | None advertised: no real-server validation, source export not advertised (VERIFIED compare page) | Community remixing, leaderboards, claimed 500k+ players (vendor claim) | Opaque quality; closed output |
| **MCreator** | Forge/NeoForge/Fabric/Bedrock via visual editor; AI only via extensions | Free, open source (VERIFIED compare page) | Decade of history | Offline, visual control, huge community | Manual assembly, desktop learning curve; AI not core (VERIFIED compare page). Details of its AI extensions: UNVERIFIED |
| **Mod Builder (stork.ai listing)** | Mods | Freemium; Pro GBP5/mo or GBP99 once (search snippet only) | Unknown | Cheap | UNVERIFIED, thin evidence |
| **BukkitCode / Bolt.new-style agents** | Whole Bukkit plugin project from chat | Unknown | Unknown | Project-level context vs one-shot chat (search snippet, UNVERIFIED) | Unknown |
| **Plain ChatGPT/Claude** | Code text | Subscription | The standing complaint is a broken-code/fix loop that "takes 30 minutes or more" (search snippet of mineacademy.org/ai-plugins-guide; page itself returned 403, so UNVERIFIED in detail) | Free-form | No compile, no test, hallucinated or outdated APIs (UNVERIFIED generally; consistent with Cyrus's own need for version sheets) |
| **Tynker** | Skins, add-ons, mini-mods | Education subscriptions | n/a | Learning | Not production (VERIFIED compare page) |

Honest gap in evidence: I found **no** Reddit/forum threads with first-hand user reviews of these tools (searches returned vendor pages and chatbot plugins only). Treat "what users praise/complain about" as vendor-positioned, not community-verified. Recommend a manual 1-hour Reddit/Discord pass before roadmap commitments.

### White space and what "number one" requires
- Rivals sell code (jar/mod) and increasingly "boot-tested" code. **None advertise** (VERIFIED absence on compare page): generated models/textures/multiple sounds as a coherent asset set, server-pushed resource packs, an editable studio for those assets, or one-click install with rollback onto the customer's own hosted server. Orca is the closest (bundled server) but ships no asset studios advertised.
- To be credibly #1 Cyrus needs: (a) a **published, reproducible pass rate** at least equal to 98% on a public prompt set, per version, including 26.x; (b) the asset pipeline (mob = model + texture + 4-6 sounds) delivered in a pack players actually receive; (c) iterate/remix on an existing mod; (d) source + undo.

## 2. Techniques that raise correctness and cut cost

Anthropic guidance (all opened):
- **Verification is the lever.** "Give Claude a check it can run: tests, a build, a screenshot"; no check means "looks done" is the only signal. Also: have an independent fresh-context reviewer subagent, scoped to correctness only, to avoid over-engineering. VERIFIED https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
- **Spec first.** Interview then write a self-contained spec naming files/interfaces, out-of-scope items and an end-to-end verification step; execute in a fresh session. VERIFIED same URL. Maps directly to a Cyrus ModSpec (missing today per G-gaps).
- **Context engineering.** Smallest set of high-signal tokens; just-in-time retrieval over loading everything; sub-agents return 1-2k token summaries; minimal non-overlapping tools. VERIFIED https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents. Implication: replace whole-sheet injection (~15 KB per version, G-gaps) with per-feature sheet slices selected from the plan.
- **Evals.** Start with 20-50 tasks drawn from real failures; code-based graders (cheap, brittle) + model rubric + human calibration; report **pass@k** and **pass^k** (consistency); read transcripts. VERIFIED https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents. SWE-bench-style = run hidden tests, pass only if target tests pass and nothing else breaks (same page).
- **Prompt caching.** Reads cost 0.1x base (0.05x on Opus/Sonnet 5.5); 5-min write 1.25x, 1-hour write 2x; min cacheable 512 tokens on 5.5-family models; breakpoint on the last identical block; changing tools, effort or thinking settings invalidates the cache. VERIFIED https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching. Cyrus already keeps the system prompt byte-stable; check that the Claude Code CLI path actually gets cache reads (log `cache_read_input_tokens`). A 1-hour TTL suits sheets reused across a user's iteration session.
- **Effort levels** low/medium/high/xhigh/max. For Sonnet 5.5 agentic coding: start `medium` for well-specified tasks, `high` for harder ones; Haiku 5.5 default medium, `low` can skip checks; run an effort sweep on your own evals; per-message effort changes preserve the cache (beta). VERIFIED https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort. Implication: the Haiku/Sonnet/Opus classifier should also pick effort, and a well-formed ModSpec makes `medium` viable (cost cut).

Minecraft-specific verification stack (ordered cheap to expensive):
1. Structured ModSpec + recipe selection (UNVERIFIED design; consistent with sources above).
2. Compile vs real Paper jar + auto-fix loop (already exists, G-gaps).
3. Static policy scan (exists).
4. **MockBukkit unit tests** the model writes alongside the code (or test-first from the spec's acceptance criteria). MIT licence; per-version artifacts `mockbukkit-v26.1.2` exist on Maven Central and the repo's current release is `mockbukkit-v26.2` for Paper API 26.2 (VERIFIED https://github.com/MockBukkit/MockBukkit; central listing from search snippet). **Limit:** unimplemented methods throw `UnimplementedOperationException` (VERIFIED same URL), so it cannot verify rendering, resource packs, custom entities' real behaviour or NMS-level code. Use it as a fast logic gate, not the acceptance gate. Older 1.21.x coverage: repo keeps older branches "not actively patched" (VERIFIED same URL) so 1.21.1/1.21.4 may be stale; UNVERIFIED which artifacts exist for each.
5. **Disposable headless Paper boot** ("Test Flight"): load the jar, assert no startup exceptions, run commands via RCON/console. Player Games' 98.2% claim shows rivals do this (VERIFIED compare page). Cyrus has eval/rtcheck already (eclipse-temurin:21-jre, mineflayer, per-version jars, G-gaps).
6. **Protocol bot** (Mineflayer): MIT licence and supports "Minecraft 1.8 to 26.1" including 1.21.11 and 26.1 (VERIFIED https://github.com/PrismarineJS/mineflayer; 7.6k stars, active). Good for joining, running commands, checking chat/inventory/entities/GUI windows/resource-pack prompt. Cannot see textures/models. 26.2 support: UNVERIFIED.
7. LLM-judge/screenshot review for assets (UNVERIFIED approach; needs a headless client, which is costly; defer).

Cost reduction levers (ranked): sheet slicing by plan; caching with stable prefix; effort per tier; ModSpec lets Haiku/Sonnet do routine builds; verified "recipes" (parametrised, compiled-in-CI snippets for mob/GUI/particle/recipe) so the model assembles instead of inventing; cap repair loops at 2-3 and retry from a fresh context after two failed corrections (VERIFIED best-practices page); cache identical builds (hash of ModSpec).

## 3. Test Flight practicalities

- Paper 26.1+ requires **Java 25**; docs suggest a 4 GB heap for a normal server (VERIFIED https://docs.papermc.io/paper/getting-started). A test server needs far less: 1-2 GB heap with a tiny flat world, `view-distance=2`, offline-mode, no spawn chunks beyond minimal (UNVERIFIED tuning; measure it). Note the existing rtcheck image uses Java 21 (G-gaps), so 26.x needs a second Java 25 image.
- Estimated cost per run (UNVERIFIED, to be measured): ~20-45 s cold boot + 5-30 s test script, 1.0-1.5 GB RSS, 1-2 vCPU burst. A pre-generated world copied from a template and a warm Docker image keep it near the low end. On a node-2 build host this is cheap compared with the model call, but concurrency must be capped (the primary node hard-crashed from parallel builds, per memory note).
- Isolation: container, no network except loopback, read-only jar mount, CPU/mem/pids limits, hard 90 s timeout, destroy on exit. The server runs untrusted AI code, so treat it like the compile sandbox.
- Resource-pack testing needs `resource-pack` prompt acceptance from a bot; Mineflayer can observe the resource-pack packet but not render (UNVERIFIED detail).

## 4. Differentiators worth testing
- **Iterative editing ("change this mod")** on the stored ModSpec + source; rivals mostly push regenerate. Measure edit success vs full regenerate.
- **Remix** of NxLabs mods (CreativeMode has remixing/leaderboards, VERIFIED compare page; Cyrus has remix already).
- **Templates/recipes gallery** doubling as test fixtures.
- **Live preview**: one-click "try it" on a temp Test Flight server, or on the customer's own server with rollback (Cyrus already has backup + rollback; Orca's bundled test server is the rival bar).
- **Project import** (upload existing plugin source/jar for edit): UNVERIFIED demand; Mineacademy-type users (owners with existing plugins) likely want it.
- **Quality signals shown to customers**: "booted on Paper X, N tests passed, bytes scanned" badge and public pass-rate page (mirrors Player Games' differentiator).

## 5. Prioritised capability list

| # | Capability | Size | Measure |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Public **eval harness v2**: 100+ prompts, per-version matrix incl. 26.x, pass@1 / pass^3, cost per pass, repair-loop count; seed from real failed customer builds | M | pass rate per version/feature class; target >=95% pass^3 on core classes |
| 2 | **ModSpec** (typed plan: entities/items/blocks/sounds/textures/commands + acceptance criteria) feeding build and asset studios | M | spec-to-built fidelity; first-try compile rate |
| 3 | **Test Flight boot gate** (Java 21 and 25 images, RCON smoke script) and show badge | M | boot-pass %, p95 time, RAM; correlation with post-install failures |
| 4 | **Sheet retrieval** (per-feature slices + 26.x sheet) replacing whole-sheet injection; verify claims with javap in CI | M | input tokens/build; API-hallucination compile errors |
| 5 | 26.x support (Java 25 toolchain, Paper 26.x jar, MockBukkit v26.x dependency) | M | eval pass rate on 26.x vs 1.21.x |
| 6 | Cache audit + effort-by-tier + spec-driven Haiku/Sonnet routing | S | cache hit %, $/successful build, quality at each effort level |
| 7 | **Verified recipes** (mob w/ model+sounds, GUI, particles, recipes, boss, command) compiled and Test-Flown in CI | L | % of builds using a recipe; pass rate delta vs freeform |
| 8 | MockBukkit tests generated test-first for logic-heavy mods | M | bug catch rate before boot; extra token cost |
| 9 | Mineflayer scenario checks from spec (join, command, GUI, resource-pack prompt) | M | scenario pass %, flake rate |
| 10 | Iterative edit + project import | M | edit success vs regenerate; adoption |
| 11 | Reviewer-subagent pass (fresh context, correctness-only) for high-effort tier | S | defects caught per $ |
| 12 | Public quality page + badge (pass rate, versions, scan) | S | conversion and trust (A/B) |

## Could not determine
Independent user reviews (Reddit/forums) of rivals; MCreator's AI extension specifics; exact MockBukkit artifacts for each 1.21.x; real Test Flight RAM/time on our host (needs a measurement run); Mineflayer on 26.2.

# Cyrus architecture (2026-10-09)

Cyrus is Nxeon's AI mod studio: a person describes a mod, Cyrus plans, writes, compiles, safety-checks and installs it on their Nxeon game server. Four layers: the portal, a separate build service on its own VM, per-game support files, and the production plumbing around them.

## Request flow

```
Browser (studio / /cyrus demo)
   |  POST /api/cyrus/generate   (ndjson stream; client re-attaches after 30 s of silence)
   v
Nxeon portal (Next.js on the primary, blue/green behind nginx, + worker)
   |  createModBuild(): access gate -> prompt check -> suspension/game switch
   |                    -> rate limits -> token reserve -> ModBuild row
   |  svcCreate {prompt, mcVersion, tier, images}
   v
Build service (VM 88001, reached over a tunnel; image 0.5)
   |  classifier (Haiku) -> model tier -> Claude Code CLI in Docker
   |  -> Gradle compile -> auto-fix -> bytecode scan -> jar
   v
Portal: stream events + live code, then jar + source
   -> settle tokens -> generate the NxLabs mod page
   -> install on a customer's server (backup, swap, rollback)
   -> Mods tab lifecycle (on/off/update/outdated)
```

## 1. Portal (`/opt/nxeon`, Next.js)

**Studio** (`/dashboard/cyrus`): React app with a store, the game and category network map, and the prompt dock. Top bar: Cyrus entry, token chip, sound toggle.

**Access gate** (`modBuilderUser`, `lib/modbuilder/access.ts`): a private-preview account, or `cyrus_studio_public_enabled` plus a verified email.

**Request pipeline** (`lib/modbuilder/create.ts`), in order:
1. Gibberish check (`lib/cyrus/prompt-check.ts`), before any tokens are held.
2. Account suspension and per-game switch (`/admin/cyrus`).
3. Rate limits: 3 builds a minute, 20 an hour, 2 in flight.
4. Token gate (`lib/cyrus/tokens/builds.ts`): reserve 70, settle to the real cost.
5. Create the `ModBuild` row.
6. Hand off to the build service.

**Token economy** (`lib/cyrus/tokens`): `CyrusTokenAccount`, `Lot`, `Ledger`, `Reservation`. Sources: paid-server grants, Stripe plans, ad-hoc top-ups, a one-time starter grant (`cyrus_tok_starter`, default 70). The plan tier decides which models you can use. Daily caps apply, with a lower cap for new accounts. An account that has ever held tokens keeps its balance pinned in the portal.

**After a build:** `syncBuild` settles tokens and `lib/cyrus-mods/doc.ts` generates the mod's NxLabs page from its versions.

**Install** (`lib/modbuilder/install.ts`): the jar goes to the server through the Mods engine, with backup, one-copy-only and rollback.

**Lifecycle, community, admin:**
- Lifecycle: on/off, updates, outdated warnings.
- Community: listings, stars, remixes, computed community-tested badge.
- `/admin/cyrus`: moderation, users and tokens, game status.

**Public pages:**
- `/cyrus`: generated native page (`tools/nxm/native/cyrus`, regenerate with `python3 tools/nxm/port_pages.py cyrus`). React islands: live core demo, drawn-by-code texture demo, studio illustration, token, badge, sound toggle.
- `/mods/cyrus/[slug]`: public mod page and SEO template (metadata, OG/Twitter, JSON-LD, FAQ, related mods).

## 2. Build service (`services/modbuilder`, VM 88001)

- Receives builds, runs two at a time.
- A one-word Haiku call picks complexity unless the person chose a model. Katara = Haiku 4.5, Saka = Sonnet, Yakko = Opus.
- Runs the Claude Code CLI headless inside Docker (egress limited to Anthropic domains), on a single Claude login session file (`.credentials.json`, mounted outside the CLI home and denied to the model). Claude gets only Read, Write and Edit in a throwaway Gradle workspace.
- The service, not Claude, does the rest:
  - compile with Gradle against the real Paper API jar for the chosen version (offline);
  - known auto-fixes and a pre-check;
  - bytecode scan (`scan.js`: `javap -c -p -v`, whole constant pool);
  - package the jar, record usage and cost.
- On a compile or scan failure it sends Claude a short repair message and resumes the same session. Cheap models can escalate to the next tier.
- Model-facing text lives in `prompts.js`, per-version API sheets in `sheets/`, failure rules in `rules/`. The exact messages are in `cyrus-backend-prompts.md`.
- Supported today: Minecraft only, Paper 1.21.1, 1.21.4, 1.21.8, 1.21.11.
- The hardened `scan.js` is in the repo but still has to be copied to the VM and the image rebuilt.

## 3. Other games

- Each game has a support file in `lib/cyrus/games/` (versions, categories, install facts, verification notes), plus template generators (`lib/cyrus/engine/`) and validators.
- Merged: Minecraft, Terraria, Valheim, Zomboid. Unmerged branches: Rust, Palworld.
- Only Minecraft goes through the real build service. The rest produce template code with no compiler in the pipeline, so they are "coming soon".

## 4. Supporting pieces

| Area | What |
|---|---|
| Switches | `cyrus_studio_public_enabled` (studio), `cyrus_tok_live` (token economy), `cyrus_public_enabled` (`/cyrus` page), `cyrus_mods_public_enabled` (community pages), `cyrus_mod_networking_enabled` (off), `cyrus_tok_starter` |
| Assets | Texture spec + pixel renderer + resource-pack builder in `lib/cyrus/textures` (not wired to the studio yet). Sound is synthesised in the browser (`lib/cyrus/sfx.ts`), off by default |
| Build and deploy | Builds run on node-2 via `scripts/devhost`. `scripts/promote-production.sh` does the zero-downtime release; rollback with `scripts/rollback-release.sh --production` |
| Main tables | `ModBuild`, `CyrusModPage` (+ listing and community tables), token tables, `CyrusPlan` |

## Status on 2026-10-09

- Production runs release `20261009T095149Z-fd6bcb7e` (main = `fd6bcb7e53`).
- Studio, tokens, `/cyrus` and the community pages are gated off.
- To go public: copy the new `scan.js` to the VM and rebuild the image, then flip `cyrus_studio_public_enabled` and `cyrus_tok_live` together.
- `cyrus_public_enabled` and `cyrus_mods_public_enabled` stay off until `/cyrus` has been reviewed on production.

# PROMPT: finish and improve Cyrus for Minecraft, Rust, Terraria, Valheim, Zomboid and Palworld

Paste everything below the line into a fresh Claude Code session on the Nxeon primary (cwd /root). It is self-contained.

---

You are continuing the Cyrus programme for Nxeon (owner: haxkodi@gmail.com; prefers concise replies; hates anything that looks cheap or vibe-coded; Malaysia/Vietnam timezone). Cyrus is Nxeon's AI mod studio: a person describes a mod, Cyrus plans, writes, compiles, safety-checks and installs it on their Nxeon game server. Your job is to take every game on the map from its CURRENT standing to FINISHED and IMPROVED, in a safe order, without breaking what is already live.

## 0. Read first (in this order, do not skip)
1. `/root/.claude/projects/-root/memory/MEMORY.md`, then these memories in full: `nxeon-cyrus-release-pass-2026-10-09.md`, `nxeon-golive-decisions-2026-10-08.md`, `nxeon-cyrus-v6-programme.md`, `nxeon-build-host-node2.md`, `nxeon-pkill-nextstart-incident.md`, `nxeon-never-reuse-vmids.md`.
2. `/root/agent-notes/BUILD-HOST.md`, `/root/agent-notes/cyrus-release-backlog.md`, `/root/agent-notes/cyrus-backend-prompts.md` (exactly what the build service sends to Claude today).
3. Per-game notes: `/root/agent-notes/cyrus-v6/game-{rust,palworld,terraria,valheim,zomboid}/` (READINESS.md and PAUSED.md in each), `/root/agent-notes/cyrus-v6/library/PAUSED.md`, `/root/agent-notes/cyrus-v6/capabilities/THREAT-MODEL.md`.
4. Code: `lib/cyrus/games/support.ts` (the GameSupport contract) and one file per game in `lib/cyrus/games/`, `lib/cyrus/engine/` (template generators), `lib/cyrus/data.ts` (the six-game registry), `lib/cyrus/categories.ts`, `lib/cyrus/game-status.server.ts`, `lib/modbuilder/*`, `services/modbuilder/*` (the build service), `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` sections "Cyrus release pass", "Cyrus v6: ..." per game.

## 1. Ground truth today (2026-10-09) — verify, do not trust
- **Live in production now:** release `20261009T095149Z-fd6bcb7e` (main = integ/golive `fd6bcb7e53`). Studio, tokens, marketing page, mod pages are built but GATED OFF until the owner flips `cyrus_studio_public_enabled` + `cyrus_tok_live` (flags `cyrus_public_enabled` and `cyrus_mods_public_enabled` stay off until the owner reviews `/cyrus`).
- **Only Minecraft really builds.** The build service (VM 88001, `services/modbuilder`, image 0.5, reached over a tunnel via `MODBUILDER_URL`) runs the Claude Code CLI headless in Docker with Read/Write/Edit only, compiles with Gradle against the real Paper API (JDK 21), scans bytecode with `scan.js`, and returns a jar. Versions: 1.21.1, 1.21.4, 1.21.8, 1.21.11. For every OTHER game the studio today produces template code from `lib/cyrus/engine/*` ("template preview"), nothing is compiled by a real toolchain in the pipeline, and no game is installable.
- **GameSupport files exist and are merged** for Minecraft, Terraria, Valheim, Zomboid. **Rust and Palworld are NOT merged**: branches `feature/cyrus-v6-game-rust` (a6cf731b0c) and `feature/cyrus-v6-game-palworld` (c91c296099), both paused. Pattern library `feature/cyrus-v6-library` (c4b5dd6288) is also unmerged.

# Executive decision

Cyrus does not need a rebuild from scratch. It already has the foundation most early AI code tools lack: a portal request pipeline, access gates, rate limits, token reservations and settlement, a separate build service, bounded concurrency, version-specific Paper API compilation, automatic repair, static bytecode scanning, immutable-ish build artifacts, a Mods installation path with backup and rollback, NxLabs pages, and the early pieces of Texture Studio and SFX Studio.

The next update should **turn that foundation into a measurably reliable mod product**. The update should concentrate on five outcomes:

1. **Security and launch readiness:** deploy and test the hardened scanner; prove workspace and build isolation; protect the build toolchain; make launch flags fail closed.
2. **Actual correctness:** add automated functional checks in addition to compilation and static scanning, beginning with MockBukkit tests and a disposable Paper startup lane.
3. **Resilience and economics:** durable job status and event replay; safe recovery and cancellation; accurate cost/quality telemetry; model routing tuned from evidence.
4. **Knowledge and edits:** version-aware retrieval from existing mods and API sheets; project manifests and revisions; surgical patches that preserve unrelated behavior; a measured self-improvement loop.
5. **Product expansion on a sound core:** integrate the existing texture renderer and sound synthesis into projects with deterministic, game-aware exports; then grow additional game adapters only when they can build and validate real artifacts.

The central operating principle is: **measure before adding complexity**. The first architectural investment should be a benchmark suite that tells us whether a change makes Cyrus better, cheaper, safer, or faster. Anthropic's current agent-evaluation guidance recommends combining deterministic checks, model-based rubrics, human review where needed, and regression suites, while tracking latency and token usage [R01].

## 6.3 Treat all mod sources as untrusted

For uploaded ZIPs, source repositories, JARs, and community remixes:
- impose archive file-count, total-uncompressed-size, per-file-size, and nesting limits;
- normalize paths and reject traversal, absolute paths, symlinks escaping the root, and duplicate-path ambiguity;
- do not execute build scripts at ingestion;
- run extractors in an isolated process and treat decompilation output as untrusted;
- capture source URL/hash, author/license, upload consent, applicable usage restrictions, and retrieval rights;
- separate proprietary user projects from global shared knowledge unless explicit opt-in permits sharing;
- do not copy large code sections from a project with an incompatible license merely because it scores high in vector search.

## 6.4 Production flags and release evidence

Add a single fail-closed launch readiness condition if practicable, or a central guard that prevents Studio from accepting a build unless both studio and token conditions are valid. The stated intended pairing of `cyrus_studio_public_enabled` and `cyrus_tok_live` should not depend on a fragile two-click timing window.

The public launch evidence bundle should record: portal release/commit, service image digest, scanner SHA-256, Gradle/JDK versions, supported Paper version matrix, scanner fixtures, integration test outcomes, feature flag values, and rollback command verification. # 9. Versioned project state and incremental editing

## 9.1 Every project gets a manifest and revision history

Create a canonical project manifest (JSON or a validated DB record) with:
- project/mod ID and owner/tenant scope;
- game, edition, mod framework, server/client mode, target version;
- build image/toolchain ID, Gradle/JDK/API versions;
- file tree with content hashes and role (`source`, `test`, `metadata`, `asset`, `generated`);
- approved dependencies and their checksums;
- feature requirements and non-goals;
- current test plan and latest test results;
- current artifact hash and artifact location;
- last known passing revision, parent revision and change summary;
- asset provenance/license records;
- model/prompt/router versions used for the build;
- installed target/version and last install/rollback state where applicable.

Store code/project revisions as an append-only history or version-controlled snapshots. Never overwrite the only known-good artifact with an untested candidate.

## 9.2 Minimal patch workflow

When a user asks for a change:
1. Load the manifest and last passing revision.
2. Parse the request into changed requirements and explicit non-goals.
3. Resolve affected symbols/files by symbol search, import/call graph, and project metadata.
4. Retrieve only the relevant source fragments, relevant API sheet, nearby tests, and directly related configuration/assets.
5. Create a patch against the existing revision, not a fresh unrelated project.
6. Check changed paths and diff size against the task spec. Flag surprising changes.
7. Run the full relevant test matrix and full project compile; run a full final artifact scan.
8. Save a new immutable revision, with a diff and reason for each changed file.
9. If tests fail, repair only the target revision; if the retry budget expires, preserve and expose the prior passing version.

## 9.3 Context packaging

Context engineering is not “put as much as possible in the prompt.” Current research emphasizes the finite nature of context and the need to curate the most useful state each turn [R02]. For Cyrus, rank context in this order: direct user requirement and non-goals; current relevant source and tests; exact version/API facts; closely matched validated examples; project decisions; only then broader history. Add file paths, source hashes, and a short reason each item was retrieved.

Avoid sending full source trees, full mod archives, and giant `MEMORY.md` files. Keep the memory store structured and retrievable. A one-page current project brief is a navigation/index document, not the authoritative project state.

# 10. Mod library retrieval and safe self-improvement

## 10.3 Ingesting the user's mod folder

Create a private “Import knowledge” job:
- User confirms they have rights to use the source for the selected purpose.
- Safely unpack in quarantine with size/path/symlink limits.
- Detect likely game/framework/version from metadata, manifest and dependency declarations; ask for confirmation where confidence is low.
- Extract source and metadata without running scripts.
- Build the file tree/symbol graph; record hashes and provenance.
- Identify licenses at the project and file level; if absent or ambiguous, mark “unknown / not eligible for shared reuse”.
- Compile/test only in a separate isolated lane and only if allowed; do not assume uploaded code is safe.
- Store as `unverified`; promote individual patterns only after independent validation.

Avoid indexing entire binary JARs as language text. For a JAR without source, metadata and decompiled code may be useful for navigation where legally appropriate, but do not reuse substantial decompiled code automatically.

## 10.4 The experience-learning loop

For each build, capture the input spec, retrieved sources, relevant diff, build/test/scanner outcomes, repair diagnostics, final artifact hash, and user acceptance signal. A summarizer can propose a compact lesson, but it enters the candidate queue—not trusted memory.

A lesson is promoted only after:
- duplicate/signature detection;
- provenance and license/consent checks;
- validation against the original failing case;
- testing on at least one different compatible case, where applicable;
- no regression in relevant test suites;
- a clear scope/version label and a confidence/trust state.

Use statuses such as `candidate`, `validated`, `deprecated`, and `rejected`. A lesson expires or gets revalidated when its API/version dependency changes. Start with retrieval and verified examples; postpone fine-tuning until you can prove the curated dataset is licensed, deduplicated, private-data-safe, and gives measurable uplift over the retrieval baseline.

- Acceptance: one redacted JSON/Markdown evidence artifact is attached to the release; values read from deployed services, not inferred from branch HEAD.

**CYR-002 — Hardened scanner rollout**
- Copy the intended `scan.js` to the VM; rebuild the image; verify in-container hash.
- Acceptance: deployed scanner hash matches approved source; image version/digest recorded; fixture suite runs against that image.

**CYR-003 — Scanner security fixture suite**
- Build known-bad and benign bytecode/JAR fixtures with expected outcomes.
- Acceptance: no false negatives in the agreed critical set; benign compatibility fixtures tracked; a scanner change cannot deploy when fixtures fail.

**CYR-004 — Immutable Gradle toolchain**
- Make project build files/wrapper/dependency policy service-owned; enforce write-path allowlist.
- Acceptance: model write to protected path is impossible/blocked and logged; tampered build script never reaches Gradle.

**CYR-005 — Sandbox audit**
- Inspect effective Docker settings, user, mounts, capabilities, namespaces, egress, resources and cleanup.
- Acceptance: automated smoke test demonstrates boundaries; timeout and cancel kill child processes; worker cannot access other job workspaces.

**CYR-006 — Launch flag guard**
- Prevent accepting public builds unless Studio/token state is valid as a pair; leave public pages gated pending review.
- Acceptance: all combinations fail closed except explicitly approved pair; audit event emitted on flag change.

## P1 — Correctness and reliability

**CYR-010 — Benchmark harness v1**
- Store task fixtures, expected outcomes, run metadata, graders and aggregate reports.
- Acceptance: same commit can repeat a benchmark; reports compare baseline and candidate with per-task diffs.
# 20. Acceptance thresholds to agree before launch

Thresholds below are suggested launch policies, not claims about current performance. Adjust them after the baseline measurement, then keep them fixed during release comparisons.

- **Security:** all critical scanner fixtures pass; no protected build file or secret exposure; every package gets a final scan; security failures cannot be auto-accepted.
- **Functional quality:** every public “feature-tested” claim has corresponding passing evidence; no required test stage is silently skipped.
- **Build reliability:** no unexplained terminal states; the final artifact hash must be the same one that passed validation and one installed by the Mods engine.
- **Job reliability:** reconnect/worker-crash/duplicate-callback tests preserve one job, one settlement outcome, and a clear terminal state.
- **Edit reliability:** no regression to known passing behavior in the protected edit suite; out-of-scope modifications are surfaced and reviewed.
- **Compatibility:** each supported version has a passing version-specific smoke test; preview versions never appear as fully supported.
- **Cost:** report median and P95 cost per accepted mod by task class; budgets cap retry/escalation even if success isn't reached.
- **Assets:** dimensions/format/mapping/metadata validate; license/provenance fields exist for imported assets; pack loads or is clearly marked untested.
- **Public launch:** current feature flags and review approvals are captured in the evidence bundle; public pages remain off until the defined review is complete.

# 21. Risks and mitigations

| Risk | Why it matters | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Scanner not deployed or untested | Source repository may be safer than running production image | Hash check, rebuild, fixture tests, deployment evidence |
| Compile success mistaken for behavior success | Plugin may load but fail the requested behavior | Test spec + MockBukkit + disposable Paper lane |
| Model edits build scripts | Build execution surface expands beyond intended source generation | Allowlisted write paths and immutable toolchain |
| Prompt injection in imported mods/docs | Retrieved instructions can manipulate tool behavior | Treat content as data, isolate tools/files/network, provenance and sanitization |
| Memory poisoning | One bad result corrupts future builds | Candidate/trusted states and cross-task validation |
| License infringement | Code/assets get reused without rights | Provenance, license-aware retrieval and sharing consent |
| Version drift | API, Java, resource pack, and Gradle requirements evolve independently | Central registry and versioned regression suite |
| Overbuilt agent orchestration | Cost/latency and failure modes grow before benefit is proven | Single-agent baseline; specialist A/B testing |
| Cache poisoning/cross-tenant leakage | Reused output/context could contaminate jobs | Key by all material inputs and tenant boundary; isolate untrusted artifacts |
| Token accounting drift | Reservation/settlement mismatch affects trust and profitability | Idempotency, reconciliation, and separate cost categories |
| False community confidence | Stars or one successful install imply more than they prove | Evidence-backed, separate badge levels |
| Asset looks right but is invalid | Preview masks wrong format/path/mapping | Deterministic export validators and target-version test |
| Queue overload | User experience and provider costs become unpredictable | Admission control, bounded concurrency and transparent statuses |

# 22. Explicitly do not build yet

- No fine-tuning pipeline until retrieval/validation is measured and a rights-cleared dataset exists.
- No global writable memory file available to every agent/session.
- No large multi-agent network before specialist roles prove value in benchmark A/B tests.
- No new vector database until current scale/latency requires it; baseline lexical/symbol search first.
- No random live prompt rewriter before an offline prompt experiment demonstrates uplift.
- No new game advertised as fully supported solely because the support file or template generator is merged.
- No entire third-party pixel editor or DAW embedded before a product prototype proves the value and license fit.
- No install/“success” status based solely on file copy or compilation.
- No auto-repair loop that can weaken security policy to satisfy the compiler or scanner.
- No broad caching of generated packages until keys include source hash, game/version, toolchain, dependencies, prompt/model/version inputs as appropriate, and user privacy boundary.

# Packwiz Overview

**What is Packwiz:**
Packwiz is "a command line tool for editing and distributing Minecraft modpacks, using a git-friendly TOML format." Rather than directly managing JAR files, it creates metadata files suitable for version control.

**File Format:**
The project uses TOML-based metadata files (pack.toml, index.toml, .pw.toml references are evident from the directory structure). This format is designed to be "easily version-controlled and shared with git."

**Mod Repository Support:**
It integrates with both CurseForge and Modrinth, enabling "easy installation and updating of multiple mods at once" from these platforms. The tool can export to both formats and import from CurseForge packs.

**Hash Handling & Export:**
Packwiz supports "creation of remote file metadata from JAR files for CurseForge mods" and can export modpacks to CurseForge and Modrinth formats (.mrpack/.curseforge zip).

**License:**
The project is licensed under the MIT license, permitting commercial and private use with minimal restrictions.

**Suitability for Hosted Services:**
The git-friendly TOML structure and HTTP server distribution capabilities suggest it could work as a library/format for hosted services, though packwiz itself is primarily a command-line tool rather than an embedded library.

# Beet: Minecraft Pack Development Kit

## Purpose
Beet addresses limitations in authoring Minecraft resource and data packs. As stated in the repository, it "unifies data pack and resource pack tooling into a single pipeline," allowing seamless integration of generators, pre-processors, and frameworks.

## Pipeline Model
The toolchain uses a plugin-based architecture. Developers can "compose plugins that can inspect and edit the generated resource pack and data pack" to implement workflows ranging from basic pack creation to advanced linting, asset generation, and function pre-processing.

## Merge Behavior
The documentation doesn't explicitly detail merge strategies for packs, though it mentions the ability to "create, read, edit and merge resource packs and data packs" as core library features.

## License & Language
Beet is licensed under MIT and developed in Python, as evidenced by its pip distribution and plugin examples using Python syntax.

## Versioning & Format Support
The provided content doesn't specify support for pack format 26.x or document a versioning scheme.

## Caching & Incremental Builds
The toolkit emphasizes performance through a "fast and lazy by default" approach where "files are transparently loaded when needed." A cache command exists (`beet cache`), though specific incremental build details aren't elaborated in this excerpt.

# Geyser's Custom Item Mapping System

## How Mapping Works

Geyser maps Java custom items to Bedrock through a correspondence system. Java items use `item_model` components (1.21.4+) or legacy `custom_model_data` values, while Bedrock custom items are pre-defined. According to the documentation, "Geyser has a mapping system that allows mapping custom Bedrock items to modified vanilla Java items."

Each mapping connects a vanilla Java item with specific component data to a Bedrock custom item definition containing pre-configured properties.

## Required Setup

**Mapping Files or API:**
Two approaches exist:
- JSON mapping files (format_version 2) listing item definitions
- Geyser extensions using the Geyser API and `GeyserDefineCustomItemsEvent`

**Bedrock Resource Pack:**
Yes, a Bedrock Edition resource pack is mandatory. Importantly, "Geyser does not convert resource packs from Java Edition, and also does not generate custom item mappings automatically." You must create the resource pack manually, containing `item_texture.json` and custom textures in the `textures/items/` folder.

## Conversion Tool

**Rainbow** is mentioned as an "automatic tool" that "make[s] converting content simpler" from Java to Bedrock formats.

## License

The documentation doesn't specify Geyser's license within this page, though the project is available on GitHub. For licensing information, consult the official GeyserMC repository directly.

## Modrinth Modpack Format (.mrpack)

The Modrinth modpack format (.mrpack) is a simple format that lets you store modpacks, and is the only format of modpack that can be uploaded to Modrinth.

## Key Fields in modrinth.index.json

The main configuration file contains these essential fields:

- **formatVersion**: The version of the format, stored as a number. The current value at the time of writing is 1.

- **game**: The game of the modpack, stored as a string. The only available type is minecraft.

- **versionId**: A unique identifier for this specific version of the modpack.

- **name**: Human-readable name of the modpack.

- **summary**: (optional) A short description of this modpack.

## Files Array

The files array contains a list of files for the modpack that needs to be downloaded. Each item contains a path field - the destination path of this file, relative to the Minecraft instance directory. For example, mods/MyMod.jar resolves to .minecraft/mods/MyMod.jar.

The hashes of the file specified must contain the SHA1 hash and the SHA512 hash.

The official documentation is available at https://docs.modrinth.com/modpacks/format for more detailed information.

# Summary

**Does this repo contain Weld?**
Yes. The repository description states it is "The python package for all things Smithed. Includes weld, cli, and libraries."

**How does Weld merge packs?**
The page provides limited technical details. It describes Weld as "The fastest pack merger of the west 🚅, build on beet technologies™" and references documentation at the wiki, but doesn't explain the specific merging mechanisms for resource packs, data packs, or individual file types like sounds.json, lang files, fonts, atlases, models, tags, or functions.

**License**
The repository is under the MIT license, as indicated in the repository sidebar.

For detailed technical information about how Weld handles specific pack components, you would need to consult the full documentation linked at https://wiki.smithed.dev/weld/.

# Paper Dialog API Summary

## Minecraft Version Requirement
The API requires **Minecraft 1.21.7 or later**, as dialogs were introduced in 1.21.6 and Paper's developer API arrived in 1.21.7.

## Dialog Types
Five dialog types are available:
- **Notice**: Single button dialog
- **Confirmation**: Two-button yes/no format
- **Dialog List**: Opens specified dialogs
- **Multiple Actions**: Displays multiple buttons
- **Server Links**: Custom server link display

## Input Controls
Four input mechanisms exist for gathering data:
- Boolean checkboxes
- Single-option dropdowns
- Text input fields
- Number range sliders

## Creating and Showing Dialogs
Developers use `Dialog.create()` with a consumer to build dialogs dynamically, or register them during bootstrap for registry access. The API requires specifying both a dialog base (containing title, body, inputs) and a type. Display occurs via `Audience#showDialog(DialogLike)` or the `/dialog show` command.

## Callbacks and Data Handling
Plugins handle button clicks through `PlayerCustomClickEvent` listeners or inline `DialogActionCallback` instances. Input retrieval uses `DialogResponseView` with getter methods like `getFloat()`. Optional NBT payloads can attach custom data to actions.

## Limitations and Notes
No experimental warnings appear in the documentation. Dialogs can be shown during "configuration phase or normal gameplay," offering versatility. The "intended way" to close dialogs uses `Audience#closeDialog()`; alternatives exist but are noted as less formal.

# Hangar Publishing Summary

Based on the provided documentation, here's what's covered:

## Publishing to Hangar

**Method:** The documentation describes using the Hangar Publish Gradle plugin for automated publishing.

**Key Steps:**
- Configure `gradle.properties` with platform versions
- Set up the `hangarPublish` block in `build.gradle.kts`
- Create a `Snapshot` release channel in your Hangar project
- Generate a Hangar API token with `create_version` permission
- Store the token as a GitHub Actions repository secret (`HANGAR_API_TOKEN`)
- Optionally automate via GitHub Actions workflows

**Features:** The plugin supports multiple platforms (Paper, Velocity, Waterfall), dependency declarations, automatic changelog generation from git commits, and resource page updates.

## Fetching Plugins & API Information

**Not Covered:** The documentation does not provide information about:
- API base URLs
- Public API endpoints for project versions or downloads
- Authentication methods for fetching plugins
- Rate limits
- Platform naming conventions
- Content policies (AI restrictions, licensing requirements, open-source mandates)

The page focuses exclusively on the *publishing* workflow for plugin developers, not on consuming or retrieving plugins from the repository.

# Modrinth API Summary

## Base URL
Production: `api.modrinth.com` | Staging: `staging-api.modrinth.com`

## Authentication
Personal access tokens (PATs) via `Authorization` header. Most requests don't require authentication—only those that create/modify data or access private information need tokens with specific scopes.

## User-Agent Requirement
**Mandatory.** Must be unique and identify your application. Poor examples (e.g., `okhttp/4.9.3`) risk traffic blocking. Recommended format: `username/project_name/version (contact_info)`.

## Rate Limits
300 requests per minute per IP. Response headers indicate `X-Ratelimit-Limit`, `X-Ratelimit-Remaining`, and `X-Ratelimit-Reset`.

## Key Endpoints
- **Versions:** List, get, create, modify versions
- **Dependencies:** Retrieve all project dependencies
- **Hash Lookup:** Query versions by SHA1/SHA512 file hash; supports bulk requests
- **Loaders List:** Available via `/tags/loaders` endpoint (no Paper/Spigot/Bukkit/Purpur/Folia mentioned)

## Commercial/Server-side Use
The documentation excerpt provided does not address commercial licensing or server-side usage restrictions. Consult the [Terms of Service](https://modrinth.com/legal/terms) for licensing details.

# Resource Pack Methods in Player API

## Method Signatures

**addResourcePack:**
```java
void addResourcePack(UUID id, String url, byte[] hash, String prompt, boolean force)
```
"Request that the player's client download and include another resource pack."

**removeResourcePack:**
```java
void removeResourcePack(UUID id)
```
"Request that the player's client remove a resource pack sent by the server."

**removeResourcePacks:**
```java
void removeResourcePacks()
```
"Request that the player's client remove all loaded resource pack sent by the server."

**setResourcePack (deprecated):**
Multiple overloaded versions exist but are marked deprecated in favor of the Adventure API's `Audience.sendResourcePacks(ResourcePackRequest)`.

**getResourcePackStatus:**
```java
PlayerResourcePackStatusEvent.Status getResourcePackStatus()
```
"Gets the most recent resource pack status from the player."

## Key Notes

- The `hash` parameter accepts a nullable byte array
- The `prompt` parameter is nullable  
- The `force` parameter determines whether the client must accept the pack
- Deprecated methods redirect toward Adventure API alternatives
- `getResourcePackHash()` is deprecated and "will always be null"

Based on the search results, here are some key open-source tools for detecting malware in Minecraft mod JAR files:

## PluginScan

PluginScan is a cross-platform java executable analyzer designed to detect malware and other malicious code in Minecraft plugins. It uses Kotlin multiplatform CafeBabe library to analyze class metadata and detect suspicious patterns. PluginScan can be used as website and CLI tool, with a web interface available on https://scan.rikonardo.com.

## MCAntiMalware

MCAntiMalware is a standalone Java tool that scans your server's plugin directory and flags known malware before it runs, with a detection database covering over 1000 identified threats. It's available on GitHub at OpticFusion1/MCAntiMalware and can be run directly from the command line.

## jNeedle

jNeedle is another jar malware detection tool. It has a GUI mode that's the easiest way to use it, available by downloading the jneedle-gui-xxx.jar from the release page. It also has a CLI mode for checking files or directories for malicious code.

## Jarspect

Jarspect is an AI-first security scanner for Minecraft mods that runs a 3-layer pipeline: MalwareBazaar threat intel, bytecode capability extraction, and Azure OpenAI verdict to classify .jar files as CLEAN, SUSPICIOUS, or MALICIOUS with full explanations.

# PackSquash Overview

## What It Does
PackSquash is a Minecraft: Java Edition optimizer that "applies per-file configurable lossy and lossless compression techniques" to resource and data packs. It handles PNG images, audio files, JSON, shaders, NBT structures, and language files through specialized optimizations.

## License
**AGPL-3.0** - This is a copyleft license requiring derivative works to be open-sourced under the same terms.

## Supported Formats
The tool processes:
- PNG images (with quantization and downsizing)
- Audio: Ogg, MP3, M4A, FLAC, WAV
- JSON files (.json, .jsonc, .mcmeta)
- Shader files (.vsh, .fsh, .glsl)
- NBT structure files
- Legacy .lang files
- OptiFine properties and BlockBench models

No specific version ceiling mentioned; it supports current Minecraft: Java Edition packs.

## Audio Handling
PackSquash **does not validate sounds.json**, but it does process audio files extensively: "channel mixing, downsampling, transcoding with...Vorbis encoder, pitch shifting, tag removal, silence truncation." Audio gets converted/optimized but the documentation doesn't explicitly confirm Ogg output format for all inputs.

Not addressed in the provided content.

content.content:
Extended functionality and modifications
We love how Minecraft inspires creativity in the community. Over the years, we have seen a lot of modifications that people have made to enhance their Minecraft.
By modifications (“mods”) we mean an original plug-in that extends the functionality of Minecraft but that doesn’t contain a substantial part of our copyrightable code or content. We have the final say on what constitutes a mod and what doesn’t. When you combine your mod with Minecraft, we refer to the combination as a “modded version” of Minecraft.
You may create, use, or distribute a mod if:
You distribute the mod 
only
 and not a modded version of Minecraft
The mod doesn’t create a play-to-earn function where players earn real-world or out-of-game currency or in-game currency that can be cashed out for real-world currency
The mod cannot be used to directly or indirectly verify whether a player owns or has access to out-of-game content, products, or services that affect in-game features and functions
Basically, we don’t want mods that affect players’ experience and creates scarcity of in-game content based off out-of-game conditions. For example, a mod that directly or indirectly checks a player owns an NFT to unlock skins, functions, or other in-game experiences is not ok with us.
Books and other publications
We have seen and read so many great stories created by our fans. We think it’s great that so many in the Minecraft community want to share stories based on Minecraft.
By “publications,” we mean any written and published work inspired by Minecraft.
You can create publications so long as:
You don’t use the Minecraft brand and assets anywhere on the front or back covers of your publication:
            o   Don’t use the Minecraft logo or the word “Minecraft” in letters that look like, or attempt to look like, the style of our logo
            o   Don’t use Minecraft artwork or images taken from official product packaging, merchandise, or marketing materials
            o   The name “Minecraft” can’t be the first word or dominant part of the title of your publication, the name of your publisher, or the name of a series of books
            o   You may use the name as a secondary name or secondary title
            o   You may, however, use screenshots of your original Minecraft creation (provided the overall cover doesn’t create the impression that it is an official Minecraft publication or authorized by Mojang or Microsoft)
The Minecraft name isn’t used as the first word or dominant part of the title, the name of the publisher, or the name of the series of books. The Minecraft name can be used as a secondary name or title
Your publication has enough of your own unique content to make it reasonable for people to want to invest in your publication, for example:
            o   Your publication shares a story of your adventures exploring and surviving in the world of Minecraft (we’re cool with that)
            o   Your publication is a coloring books, poster, sticker book, or chart that just copies our assets (we’re not cool with that)
Hand-crafted products
We want to encourage our fans to make, share, hand crafted toys, clothes, and other products inspired by Minecraft with the community. We have created these guidelines to help hobbyist fans share the fruits of their creative labors and even make a little money from their unique designs. What we don’t want is someone to try to commercialize our name, brand and assets or run a business selling products featuring our name, brand, or assets.
To us, a unique design is something that adds enough personal creativity to make the work distinctive and original.
You may make and sell certain individual handcrafted products that feature your unique design so long as you conform with all these additional guidelines:
The product contains enough of your own personal creativity to make it distinctive/original to be considered a unique design and does not use any of the Minecraft brand or assets as the dominant part of the product or design, for example:
A hand-crocheted blanket with the texture pattern of the Creeper (we’re cool with that)
A box that features Steve’s face in the Minecraft textures but with green eyes (we’re not cool with that)
Don’t use any of the software, music, or other audio from Minecraft as part of the product
The product is not mass produced or distributed through a major retailer
You don’t make and sell more than 20 product items using the same (or substantially similar) design, for example:
            o   You make and sell 20 T-shirts using design A and 20 T-shirts using design B (that’s ok)

I'm confirming the Minecraft usage guidelines on mods: no play-to-earn or NFT mechanics, servers must charge everyone equally with full mod access, and no gambling allowed. The EULA permits mods only if they're not sold for profit, which means a creator marketplace selling mods directly would violate the terms — the viable approach is monetizing the service layer like compute, tokens, or hosting rather than the mods themselves.

This translates into content policy rules for the scanner: block prompts related to play-to-earn, rank-selling tied to pay-to-win mechanics, and gambling features like loot boxes or crates for real money. I'm also noting the restriction against using Mojang's original music, audio, or vanilla assets in generated packs — everything should be original content, checked against vanilla files via perceptual hashing if needed.

Now I'm moving on to check more documentation sources, specifically trying to pull up the Modrinth modpack format specs through their docs or support articles since the direct fetch returned a 404.

## Resource Pack Merging Solutions

PackMerger is a Paper plugin that merges multiple Minecraft resource packs into a single pack, designed for servers that need to combine packs from different sources — UI overhauls, mechanics plugins like QualityArmory, and custom model packs — into one seamless download.

PackMerger detects packs generated by other installed plugins including Oraxen, Nexo, ItemsAdder, ModelEngine, EliteMobs, and FreeMinecraftModels and pulls each into the merge automatically. It uses format-aware deep JSON merging with dedicated strategies per Minecraft format (models, blockstates, items, equipment, atlases, font, sounds, language, pack.mcmeta).

## Individual Plugin Approaches

**Oraxen:** Oraxen provides a system to merge multiple resource packs into a single cohesive pack using two methods: ZIP file uploads or direct folder structure, both processed automatically during pack generation.

**Nexo:** Nexo dynamically merges conflicting files like a paper.json or sounds.json instead of migrating it to oraxen-configs to be generated.

## Conflict Limitations

ResourcePackManager merges where possible but cannot fix fundamental conflicts (e.g. GUI unicode spacing clashes or duplicate item model IDs), and in conflicts, the higher-priority pack is chosen.

Core shader files cannot be merged automatically; if multiple packs provide the same shader, you must resolve the conflict manually or choose which pack's shader to use.

I've found the information about the US Copyright Office Part 2 report on copyrightability. Here are the key findings regarding AI-generated outputs, prompts, and human authorship:

## Key Findings on AI-Generated Outputs and Human Authorship

Part 2 of the Report addresses the copyrightability of outputs created using generative AI. The outputs of generative AI can be protected by copyright only where a human author has determined sufficient expressive elements, which can include situations where a human-authored work is perceptible in an AI output, or a human makes creative arrangements or modifications of the output, but not the mere provision of prompts.

## Prompts Alone Are Insufficient for Copyright Protection

Based on current AI technology, prompting an AI model does not alone provide sufficient control to constitute human authorship of AI generated outputs, which means that AI output generated solely by prompts cannot be protected by copyright.

## Additional Protections and Framework

The Office confirms that the use of AI to assist in the process of creation or the inclusion of AI-generated material in a larger human-generated work does not bar copyrightability. It also finds that the case has not been made for changes to existing law to provide additional protection for AI-generated outputs.

The U.S. Copyright Office released Part 2 of its Report on the legal and policy issues related to copyright and artificial intelligence (AI) on January 29, 2025.

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive overview of the topics in your query:

## Folia Overview

Folia is a high-performance fork of Paper that implements regionised multithreading to scale Minecraft servers. Folia groups nearby loaded chunks to form an "independent region," with each independent region having its own tick loop, which is ticked at the regular Minecraft tickrate (20TPS), and the tick loops are executed on a thread pool in parallel.

## Plugin Compatibility and folia-supported Flag

Folia breaks most standard Paper plugins because it removes the single main thread, and to prevent instability, Folia will only load plugins that have been explicitly marked as compatible. To mark a plugin as compatible, add the following to your plugin.yml: folia-supported: true

## Schedulers

Folia has different types of schedulers that can be used for different things, and when you use these schedulers while running Paper, they will be internally handled to provide the same functionality as if you were running Folia. Folia's RegionScheduler and Folia's EntityScheduler allow scheduling of tasks to the "next tick" of whatever region "owns" either a location or an entity.

## Compatibility Solutions

For servers that want to run legacy plugins on Folia, FoliaForAll allows you to run your Paper plugins on Folia with no source changes required, removing barriers so that the vast majority of legacy Bukkit/Paper plugins work out of the box.

Anthropic: third parties may not "route requests through Free, Pro, or Max plan credentials on behalf of their users", and plan limits "assume ordinary, individual usage" (VERIFIED S3). | A launch-blocking terms problem and a hidden capacity cap (the weekly 99% usage you already hit). Unit economics are also computed on the wrong cost basis. | Day 1, before anything: read `/health` field `auth` on the VM (`api_key` vs `subscription`). If subscription: move to an API key under Commercial Terms, re-measure cost per build, re-price tokens. Never go public on a login file. |
| 2 | **Mojang's EULA says mods are yours "as long as you don't sell them for money / try to make money from them"** (VERIFIED S1). Usage Guidelines: charging for a server is fine only if everyone gets the same access to all enabled mods; no gambling or mature content; no play-to-earn; no mod that checks out-of-game ownership (NFT example) (VERIFIED S2). | A "creator marketplace / revenue share on mods" is the one idea here that directly contradicts the EULA text. Cyrus can sell compute, hosting and tooling, not mods. Also needs prompt-level policy (see E-20). | Drop marketplace/rev-share. Add policy classes to prompt-check: gambling/crates for real money, pay-to-win, play-to-earn, ownership-gated content, NFTs. Get counsel to confirm "token fee for generation" is not "selling a mod". |

## (D) Improvements to existing plan items

**Engine quality**
- IR: JSON Schema (portable contract) + Zod types, `schemaVersion` plus explicit migrations (the DataFixer idea), content-addressed registries. Cache key = hash(spec, registry version, generator version, toolchain digest, asset hashes); AI-authored steps are stored outputs, not re-run on replay (UNVERIFIED analogy to Unity/Godot importers; standard practice).
- Build record per artifact: engine release id (prompt version + sheets + rules + scanner hash + image digest), source hash, classpath hash, output hash, SBOM, scan report; SLSA Build L1 now ("provenance exists") and L2 with a signed attestation from the build service (levels VERIFIED S21).
- Testing: property-based (fast-check) for merge laws (idempotent, order-stable, no key loss), golden pack snapshots (canonical JSON + sorted file list + sha1), javap-verified sheets in CI, contract test of the version registry against the Fill API and the pack-format wiki, mutation corpus for conflicts (take a good mod, rename ids to collide).

**Conflict engine: classes beyond the Day-8 list**

| Class | Detection |
|---|---|
| Single-owner resources: Vault economy/permission provider, chat renderer, tab list, sidebar, join/quit messages, world border/time/weather/gamerules, GUI title glyphs, spawn handling | Bytecode registration scan + known-API table (extend `scan.js` constant-pool parse) |
| Legacy `custom_model_data` integer collisions (1.21.1) and `item_model` keys | Global allocator + registry; static scan of data components |
| Event semantics: two plugins mutate/cancel the same event at the same priority; MONITOR misuse | Register-call extraction (event class + priority); report as warn |
| Brigadier root literal and alias collisions, overrides of vanilla commands, permission default clashes | Descriptor + bytecode scan |
| Datapack: `replace:true` tags, same `minecraft:` loot/recipe id overridden twice, load/tick function tag order, enchantment/biome id collisions | JSON path index across packs |
| Resource: whole-file overrides (models, blockstates, items, shaders, pack.mcmeta), font provider codepoint overlap (PUA), unmergeable shaders, sound-event `replace:true` of vanilla events (affects all mobs), atlas sources | Path index + format-aware merge; ResourcePackManager documents shader/GUI-spacing/duplicate-model-id as unfixable (S19) |
| Budget classes: display-entity count, ticking tasks, pack size, entity cap | Spec-declared budgets summed per server |
| Platform: missing `folia-supported`, api-version/Java mismatch, mod needs 1.21.4+ item_model but server is 1.21.1 | Registry capability flags |
| Policy: Mod Pack containing a server jar ("Modded Version" distribution is forbidden, S1) | Pack validator: no vanilla/Paper binaries ever |

Resolution that is cheap and robust: **reserve a namespace per project at creation** (`nx_<short hash>`) so ids, keys, permissions, sound keys, glyph ranges and model paths are collision-free by construction; keep regeneration-with-prefix only for imports. Version resolution: plugin `depend/softdepend/loadbefore` is a DAG plus platform/Java ranges; a small custom resolver is enough (PubGrub-style solvers are overkill; UNVERIFIED).

**Import: safe ingestion**
Zip-slip and zip-bomb ratio limits, nested jar limit, multi-release and class-major checks, strip signatures, no execution; detect build system by `settings.gradle(.kts)`, `pom.xml`, `plugin.yml`/`paper-plugin.yml` location, then ignore the build files; Kotlin/Lombok/annotation processors are unsupported because `-proc:none`. Attestation record: typed name, checkbox text version, timestamp, upload hash, licence detected (SPDX scan) and licence claimed; public sharing requires consent plus a licence compatible with redistribution; jar-only imports are analysis-only. Takedown: published page with contact, strike policy, kill switch that unpublishes a page and flags installs (US designated-agent registration: UNVERIFIED, ask counsel).

**Premium studio features** (beyond the plan): 3D preview (three.js) for item display transforms and server-rendered turntables; tile preview and onion skin for animated textures; pixel palette ramps with contrast and colour-blind checks; waveform with spectrum, LUFS and true-peak readouts; per-mod **Style DNA** (palette ramps, outline rule, noise, sound mood) applied to every asset for consistency; reference-image-to-spec through a vision model that proposes palette and silhouette (not image generation); asset history with visual/waveform diffs; library search by tag first, embeddings later in the existing Postgres; mandatory subtitle keys for custom sounds (accessibility and `sounds.json` already supports `subtitle`); mobile-friendly read-only preview and approve flow (editing stays desktop).

**Quality bar:** replace "owner approves 20 samples" with a rubric plus metrics: texture (palette size, contrast ratio, edge density, banding, transparent-pixel policy), sound (mono, true peak, LUFS band per event role, silence ratio, DC offset), plus a vision-model judge calibrated against 100 owner-labelled samples, tracked per release.

**Operations**
- Test servers: 1-1.5 GB each, 20-45 s boot (UNVERIFIED, from F); cap concurrency (node-1 hard-crashed from parallel builds, memory) and reuse a warm image; run on node-2.
- Pack bandwidth: R2 egress is free (VERIFIED S20); use content-addressed immutable URLs `/p/<sha1>.zip`, `Cache-Control: immutable`, retention GC; record accept/decline via `PlayerResourcePackStatusEvent` from the Pack Loader.
- Pipeline incident/rollback: treat prompt+sheets+rules+scanner+image as one **engine release**, canary at 5%, auto-rollback on eval regression, per-feature kill switches (asset generation, import, packs).
- Model/provider risk: the whole pipeline is the Claude Code CLI (A-1 applies); add a thin provider interface for the planning step only; log cost per stage.
- Prompt injection (OWASP LLM01 indirect injection; VERIFIED S22): imported README/comments/docs enter the model only as quoted data files; the model keeps Read/Write/Edit with no network; reject diffs touching paths outside the allow-list; every output still passes compile + scan; never feed imported content into shared memory.
- Supply chain: pinned jars with sha256 (Fill API gives hashes; UNVERIFIED for plugins beyond Hangar sha256 field S7), image digests, lockfiles for studio npm deps, Mojang data-generator output kept on the build host only.

**Future games (short):** add `game` to every id and registry; ModSpec has `artifactKinds` per adapter; assets have a `kind` registry (pixel texture, mesh, audio clip, config); delivery strategy is an adapter method (server-pushed pack / client zip / none). Realistic 3D profile: glTF 2.0 mesh + PBR maps, per-game budgets and exporters (Unity asset bundles for Valheim/Rust, UNVERIFIED), 2D sprite sheets for tModLoader and Zomboid (UNVERIFIED). Build none of this now beyond the interfaces.

**Arithmetic on the research files' own sizing (UNVERIFIED, my sum):** texture MVP about 4 weeks (editor alone L), sound about 3-4, models about 6, data packs about 5, conflict engine + Mod Packs and import each L, designers L each. ## (D) Improvements to existing plan items

**Engine quality**
- IR: JSON Schema (portable contract) + Zod types, `schemaVersion` plus explicit migrations (the DataFixer idea), content-addressed registries. Cache key = hash(spec, registry version, generator version, toolchain digest, asset hashes); AI-authored steps are stored outputs, not re-run on replay (UNVERIFIED analogy to Unity/Godot importers; standard practice).
- Build record per artifact: engine release id (prompt version + sheets + rules + scanner hash + image digest), source hash, classpath hash, output hash, SBOM, scan report; SLSA Build L1 now ("provenance exists") and L2 with a signed attestation from the build service (levels VERIFIED S21).
- Testing: property-based (fast-check) for merge laws (idempotent, order-stable, no key loss), golden pack snapshots (canonical JSON + sorted file list + sha1), javap-verified sheets in CI, contract test of the version registry against the Fill API and the pack-format wiki, mutation corpus for conflicts (take a good mod, rename ids to collide).

**Conflict engine: classes beyond the Day-8 list**

| Class | Detection |
|---|---|
| Single-owner resources: Vault economy/permission provider, chat renderer, tab list, sidebar, join/quit messages, world border/time/weather/gamerules, GUI title glyphs, spawn handling | Bytecode registration scan + known-API table (extend `scan.js` constant-pool parse) |
| Legacy `custom_model_data` integer collisions (1.21.1) and `item_model` keys | Global allocator + registry; static scan of data components |
| Event semantics: two plugins mutate/cancel the same event at the same priority; MONITOR misuse | Register-call extraction (event class + priority); report as warn |
| Brigadier root literal and alias collisions, overrides of vanilla commands, permission default clashes | Descriptor + bytecode scan |
| Datapack: `replace:true` tags, same `minecraft:` loot/recipe id overridden twice, load/tick function tag order, enchantment/biome id collisions | JSON path index across packs |
| Resource: whole-file overrides (models, blockstates, items, shaders, pack.mcmeta), font provider codepoint overlap (PUA), unmergeable shaders, sound-event `replace:true` of vanilla events (affects all mobs), atlas sources | Path index + format-aware merge; ResourcePackManager documents shader/GUI-spacing/duplicate-model-id as unfixable (S19) |
| Budget classes: display-entity count, ticking tasks, pack size, entity cap | Spec-declared budgets summed per server |
| Platform: missing `folia-supported`, api-version/Java mismatch, mod needs 1.21.4+ item_model but server is 1.21.1 | Registry capability flags |
| Policy: Mod Pack containing a server jar ("Modded Version" distribution is forbidden, S1) | Pack validator: no vanilla/Paper binaries ever |

Resolution that is cheap and robust: **reserve a namespace per project at creation** (`nx_<short hash>`) so ids, keys, permissions, sound keys, glyph ranges and model paths are collision-free by construction; keep regeneration-with-prefix only for imports. Version resolution: plugin `depend/softdepend/loadbefore` is a DAG plus platform/Java ranges; a small custom resolver is enough (PubGrub-style solvers are overkill; UNVERIFIED).

**Import: safe ingestion**
Zip-slip and zip-bomb ratio limits, nested jar limit, multi-release and class-major checks, strip signatures, no execution; detect build system by `settings.gradle(.kts)`, `pom.xml`, `plugin.yml`/`paper-plugin.yml` location, then ignore the build files; Kotlin/Lombok/annotation processors are unsupported because `-proc:none`. Attestation record: typed name, checkbox text version, timestamp, upload hash, licence detected (SPDX scan) and licence claimed; public sharing requires consent plus a licence compatible with redistribution; jar-only imports are analysis-only. Takedown: published page with contact, strike policy, kill switch that unpublishes a page and flags installs (US designated-agent registration: UNVERIFIED, ask counsel).

**Premium studio features** (beyond the plan): 3D preview (three.js) for item display transforms and server-rendered turntables; tile preview and onion skin for animated textures; pixel palette ramps with contrast and colour-blind checks; waveform with spectrum, LUFS and true-peak readouts; per-mod **Style DNA** (palette ramps, outline rule, noise, sound mood) applied to every asset for consistency; reference-image-to-spec through a vision model that proposes palette and silhouette (not image generation); asset history with visual/waveform diffs; library search by tag first, embeddings later in the existing Postgres; mandatory subtitle keys for custom sounds (accessibility and `sounds.json` already supports `subtitle`); mobile-friendly read-only preview and approve flow (editing stays desktop).

**Quality bar:** replace "owner approves 20 samples" with a rubric plus metrics: texture (palette size, contrast ratio, edge density, banding, transparent-pixel policy), sound (mono, true peak, LUFS band per event role, silence ratio, DC offset), plus a vision-model judge calibrated against 100 owner-labelled samples, tracked per release.

**Operations**
- Test servers: 1-1.5 GB each, 20-45 s boot (UNVERIFIED, from F); cap concurrency (node-1 hard-crashed from parallel builds, memory) and reuse a warm image; run on node-2.
- Pack bandwidth: R2 egress is free (VERIFIED S20); use content-addressed immutable URLs `/p/<sha1>.zip`, `Cache-Control: immutable`, retention GC; record accept/decline via `PlayerResourcePackStatusEvent` from the Pack Loader.
- Pipeline incident/rollback: treat prompt+sheets+rules+scanner+image as one **engine release**, canary at 5%, auto-rollback on eval regression, per-feature kill switches (asset generation, import, packs).
- Model/provider risk: the whole pipeline is the Claude Code CLI (A-1 applies); add a thin provider interface for the planning step only; log cost per stage.
- Prompt injection (OWASP LLM01 indirect injection; VERIFIED S22): imported README/comments/docs enter the model only as quoted data files; the model keeps Read/Write/Edit with no network; reject diffs touching paths outside the allow-list; every output still passes compile + scan; never feed imported content into shared memory.
- Supply chain: pinned jars with sha256 (Fill API gives hashes; UNVERIFIED for plugins beyond Hangar sha256 field S7), image digests, lockfiles for studio npm deps, Mojang data-generator output kept on the build host only.

**Future games (short):** add `game` to every id and registry; ModSpec has `artifactKinds` per adapter; assets have a `kind` registry (pixel texture, mesh, audio clip, config); delivery strategy is an adapter method (server-pushed pack / client zip / none). Realistic 3D profile: glTF 2.0 mesh + PBR maps, per-game budgets and exporters (Unity asset bundles for Valheim/Rust, UNVERIFIED), 2D sprite sheets for tModLoader and Zomboid (UNVERIFIED). Build none of this now beyond the interfaces.

## (G) Cut list, must-keep, and a realistic schedule

**Arithmetic on the research files' own sizing (UNVERIFIED, my sum):** texture MVP about 4 weeks (editor alone L), sound about 3-4, models about 6, data packs about 5, conflict engine + Mod Packs and import each L, designers L each. Days 3-11 as written equal roughly 25-35 engineer-weeks. Even with agents, the real limiters are the owner-only steps, (T) real-client tests, usage allowance and node capacity. **Sixteen days is not credible for the full list; it is credible for the foundation plus one asset slice.**

**Must keep (in this order)**
1. Auth/ToS fix; launch gates (scan live, flag guard, per-build record, abuse limit, cost cap).
2. Version registry (exact pack formats, JDK, classpath, capabilities) + 26.x lane on javac; reproducible jar.
3. ModSpec/project model + revision store + identifier registry with reserved namespaces + GameAdapter interface.
4. Pack hosting + Pack Loader + managed-plugin mechanism + Test Flight lite (boot, RCON, datapack/pack checks).
5. Texture slice (items, the Glock) and sound slice (library tags, server-side Ogg, `sounds.json`, subtitles), with server-side gates and the access test matrix.
6. Server inventory + static conflict engine + Mod Pack manifest installed/rolled back as one unit (reference third-party jars by hash).
7. Import: source-only with allowlist, attestation, strict vs attested scan.
8. Datapack MVP: recipes, loot, advancements, tags, functions, enchantments with per-version emitters and the boot check.
9. Eval harness extension (100+ prompts, per-version matrix, asset prompts) with a public pass-rate page.

**Cut or defer**
- Full creature pipeline (Day 5): defer to after 26.x lane is stable; ship "skin + full sound set on a vanilla mob" and static item models now.
- Gameplay Designers 1 and 2 (ability graph, quest/boss/GUI builders): each is a mini-language; defer. Keep only "edit parameters of a generated mod".
- Biomes/structures/worldgen (Data Pack Studio phase 2): defer.
- Full pixel/sound editors: ship an iframe or minimal editor stopgap (miniPaint MIT per C) and wavesurfer trim/fade; build the real editor on demand.
- Namespace-regeneration resolution for arbitrary imports; dynamic pairwise combined scenario tests; AI image/audio providers; Bedrock conversion; marketplace; Day 14 extras (screenshot-to-mod, structure generator, simulation); Day 15 other games (own programme); Day 16 Fabric; 1.21.1/1.21.4 retirement decision by usage data; core-shader HUDs (A already says avoid).

**Suggested sequence:** R0 foundation (about Days 1-4 of work) -> R1 asset slice (about Days 5-9) -> R2 composition + datapacks + import (about Days 10-16). Realistic calendar for R0-R2 including owner waits: 5-7 weeks (UNVERIFIED judgement).

Full report is at /root/agent-notes/cyrus-research/GAPS-AND-IDEAS.md. It runs about 5,400 words, over the ~4,500 target. I read all the files, then opened about 40 pages and APIs. The claims are labelled VERIFIED with a source key, or UNVERIFIED. It follows your A–H structure.

Top 10 findings:
1. **Possible terms violation:** the build service (server.js:26, entrypoint.sh, the architecture doc) can run on a Claude subscription login. Anthropic's legal page forbids routing customer requests through Free/Pro/Max credentials. Check the VM `/health` `auth` field. If it says `subscription`, switch to an API key and re-price tokens before launch.
2. **Mojang EULA conflict:** the EULA says mods are yours only if you don't sell them or try to make money from them. A creator marketplace or revenue share on mods contradicts that. The Usage Guidelines also ban gambling, play-to-earn and ownership-gated mods. Drop the marketplace and add a policy classifier to the prompt check.
3. **Modrinth bans primarily AI-generated uploads** (since 2026-08-13). `.mrpack` has no Paper loader ID. Use your own manifest shaped like mrpack, and treat NxLabs as the only channel.
4. **Day order has dependency inversions:** Test Flight (Day 12) is needed by Days 7 and 8. The version registry (Day 13) is needed by Days 1–3. Server inventory (Day 14) is needed by the conflict engine (Day 8). The research files' own S/M/L sizes sum to roughly 25–35 engineer-weeks for Days 3–11, so 16 days is not credible. I give a re-sequence and cut list: defer the creature pipeline, the Gameplay Designers, other games and Fabric.
5. **server.properties holds one pack only.** Paper's `Player#addResourcePack(UUID, …)` allows several, and `setResourcePack` is deprecated. Build a managed Nxeon Pack Loader plugin rather than merging packs by hand. Weld and Beet (both MIT) are merge prior art.
6. **BetterModel is split in two:** v3 needs Java 25 and covers 1.21.4–26.3, while v2 is Java 21, covers 1.21.x, and has been stale since March. A banshee on 1.21.x isn't realistic, so make it a 26.x feature first.
7. **Import is much harder than one day.** Compile is plain `javac -proc:none` on a Paper-only classpath, and the scanner bans reflection and network. Imports need a pinned dependency allowlist and a looser scan profile for owner-attested uploads.
8. **26.x is cheaper than estimated** because compile is javac, not Gradle. But Paper 26.3's newest build is BETA, so pin an exact stable build. Jars aren't reproducible because `jar --create` has no `--date`.
9. **Plan-tier gating needs a rule:** gate creating and editing assets, never installing or keeping them. Fail closed when the token economy is off.
10. **Licences:** paper-api is GPL-3.0, Citizens is OSL-3.0, and PackSquash is AGPL. A US Copyright Office report says prompt-only output isn't copyrightable. The owner's 514 sound files can be extracted from every pack, so their provenance and customer licence need to be written down.

The file also covers ranked new features, risks, and 10 questions for you.
